title: Accessibility basics
canDo: make your app usable for everyone

blocks.md: You ship your portfolio project. It looks great — clean layout, smooth animations. Then someone tries to use it with only a keyboard and gets completely stuck. A screen-reader user hears "button button button" with no clue what any of them do. A person with low vision can't read the light-grey text on white. None of this is exotic edge-case territory — roughly 1 in 5 people have some form of disability that affects how they use the web. Accessibility (a11y) is not a bolt-on feature; it is the measure of whether your app actually works.

blocks.md: **Quick audit you can do right now.** Open your project and press Tab repeatedly without touching the mouse. Can you reach every button, link, and input? Can you activate each one with Enter or Space? If your focus indicator disappears or the tab order jumps around unpredictably, that is the first thing to fix. This keyboard-only walk-through costs two minutes and catches the most common failures.

questions.question: What does web accessibility (a11y) mean in practice?
options: Making your app load faster for users on slow connections
Ensuring your app works for people regardless of how they interact with it, including keyboard, screen reader, and other assistive technologies
Adding high-contrast colour themes as an optional setting
Passing a Google Lighthouse performance score above 90
questions.explanation: Accessibility means your app is usable by people with a wide range of abilities and interaction methods — keyboard-only users, screen-reader users, people with low vision, and more.

questions.question: Why do form inputs need a `<label>` element (or `aria-label`), and why does image alt text matter?
options: Labels and alt text are only needed for legal compliance; sighted users benefit from neither
Without a label a screen reader can only announce the input type; without alt text it announces the filename — both leave blind users without useful information
Labels improve CSS styling; alt text is used by search engines but has no accessibility effect
They are optional when the placeholder attribute is present, which screen readers read equally well
questions.explanation: Screen readers rely on labels to describe what an input is for, and on alt text to describe images. Without them, users who cannot see the screen receive no useful information.

questions.question: A user can reach your page's navigation links by pressing Tab, but the focus outline has been removed with `outline: none` in CSS and nothing replaces it. What is the problem?
options: No problem — the element is still focusable, so keyboard navigation works correctly
The element is no longer in the tab order, so keyboard users skip it entirely
Keyboard users can reach the element but cannot tell which element is currently focused, making navigation unusable in practice
The outline removal only affects mouse users; screen readers are unaffected
questions.explanation: Removing the focus outline without a replacement means keyboard users lose the visible indicator of where focus is — they can still tab through elements, but they have no way to know which one is active.

blocks.md: Accessibility is not an afterthought — it is the baseline that makes your app usable by everyone. The five cheap wins do the heavy lifting: **semantic HTML**, **labelled inputs**, **descriptive alt text**, **visible keyboard focus**, and **sufficient colour contrast**. You do not need to memorise every WCAG rule; you need to know the W3C WAI tips page and the MDN Accessibility module so you can look up the right guidance when you build. Start with the two-minute keyboard audit on every project you ship.
bullets: Semantic HTML gives screen readers role information for free — use real `<button>`, `<nav>`, `<h1>`–`<h6>`
Every input needs a `<label>` or `aria-label`; every non-decorative image needs meaningful alt text
Keyboard users must be able to Tab to every interactive element and see which element is focused
Colour contrast of 4.5:1 minimum (WCAG AA) — verify with a contrast checker before shipping
